name: Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (LEOPARD syndrome)

reference.source: GeneReviews / Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
clinicalPearls: The historical LEOPARD acronym captures the core features: multiple Lentigines, ECG conduction abnormalities, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormal genitalia, Retardation of growth, and sensorineural Deafness
It belongs to the RASopathy family and overlaps clinically with classic Noonan syndrome, but the disproportionate cardiac and pigmentary features help separate it

Most cases arise from specific missense variants in PTPN11 that reduce SHP2 phosphatase activity, in contrast to the activating variants that typically cause classic Noonan syndrome; RAF1 and BRAF variants account for a minority
Widespread flat brown macules (lentigines) accumulate from childhood and are frequently accompanied by café-au-lait macules, whereas lentigines are not a feature of classic Noonan
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is markedly more common than in classic Noonan, while valvar pulmonary stenosis remains the characteristic right-sided lesion
Sensorineural hearing loss and genital anomalies such as cryptorchidism or hypospadias are recognised components that warrant proactive screening
Management is multidisciplinary and surveillance-based, centring on cardiology follow-up (echocardiography and ECG), audiology, growth monitoring, and developmental support
reference.pathophysiology: The condition is one of the RASopathies, a group of developmental disorders caused by dysregulation of the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway. The majority of cases result from germline missense variants in PTPN11, which encodes the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2. Unlike the gain-of-function variants underlying most classic Noonan syndrome, the variants seen here tend to impair the catalytic activity of SHP2, producing a distinct dominant effect on downstream signalling that shapes the characteristic pigmentary, cardiac, auditory, and craniofacial phenotype. A smaller proportion of patients carry variants in other pathway genes such as RAF1 or BRAF. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, and many cases represent de novo events.
additionalDifferentials: Carney complex (lentigines with cardiac myxomas and endocrine tumours)
Costello syndrome and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome (other RASopathies)
Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without syndromic features
additionalInvestigations: Targeted or panel-based molecular genetic testing for PTPN11 and related RASopathy genes
Baseline and serial echocardiography to detect hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary stenosis
Formal audiological assessment for sensorineural hearing loss
Growth monitoring with attention to short stature and consideration of endocrine review
Genital and developmental assessment, with genetic counselling for the family
redFlags: Progressive left ventricular hypertrophy or outflow obstruction on echocardiography
Syncope, arrhythmia, or high-grade conduction block suggesting cardiac decompensation
Sudden clinical deterioration in an infant with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Rapidly changing or atypical pigmented lesions requiring dermatological review
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by the cardiac phenotype: many patients have a normal or near-normal lifespan, but significant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy carries a risk of arrhythmia, heart failure, and sudden death, making lifelong cardiac surveillance essential. The lentigines are cosmetic and benign, and cognition is usually normal or only mildly affected.
pitfalls: Attributing the café-au-lait and lentiginous pigmentation to neurofibromatosis and missing the underlying RASopathy
Assuming the cardiac risk mirrors classic Noonan and under-appreciating the higher burden of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Overlooking sensorineural hearing loss because it can be subtle and progressive
Failing to arrange genetic counselling given autosomal dominant inheritance and variable expressivity
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
